title: Goalkeeper Owono Receives 12‑Match Ban Following De Miguel’s Fatal Incident, Al Jazeera Reports
body:
FC Andorra’s 22‑year‑old goalkeeper, Jesús Owón, has been handed a twelve‑match suspension after a violent clash with Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel on 2 November led to the striker’s tragic death. The Spanish Football Federation’s disciplinary committee met on Friday and imposed the longest ban ever recorded for a single incident in the country’s professional leagues, signalling a stern response to an event that has sent shockwaves through the football community.

The collision occurred in the 71st minute of the Segunda División encounter at Andorra’s Estadi Nacional. De Miguel, racing down the left flank, collided head‑first with Owón as the goalkeeper lunged to collect a high ball. The impact left the forward unconscious; he was immediately stretchered off and taken to a nearby hospital, where he later succumbed to injuries sustained to his brain. The match was abandoned after the incident, and both clubs were left grappling with the emotional fallout.

In its ruling, the disciplinary panel cited “excessive force” and “a clear breach of the duty of care owed by a goalkeeper to opposing players.” While the committee acknowledged that football is a contact sport and that accidental collisions are part of the game, it emphasized that Owón’s challenge was “recklessly dangerous” and went beyond the acceptable limits of competitive play. The twelve‑match ban, coupled with a fine of €30,000, reflects the federation’s intent to deter similar conduct and to reinforce player safety as a non‑negotiable priority.

The decision has reignited a broader debate about the adequacy of existing safety protocols in Spanish football. Critics argue that the existing medical screening and concussion management procedures are insufficient, especially in lower‑tier competitions where resources are scarcer. The Spanish league has already introduced mandatory concussion protocols for top‑flight matches, but implementation at the Segunda level has been uneven. Player unions are now calling for a uniform, league‑wide system that includes immediate on‑field neurological assessments, extended recovery periods, and stricter penalties for dangerous play.

Legal experts note that the ban could also have ramifications beyond the pitch. De Miguel’s family has signalled intentions to pursue civil action against both Owón and FC Andorra, alleging negligence. While criminal charges are unlikely, the case may set a precedent for how clubs and governing bodies address liability when a player’s life is lost due to on‑field incidents. The federation’s disciplinary body, meanwhile, has pledged to review its disciplinary guidelines to ensure they align with international best practices, including those recommended by FIFA’s Medical Committee.

For Owón, the suspension represents a career‑altering moment. The goalkeeper, who had been lauded for his reflexes and composure, now faces a protracted period away from competitive action, during which he must confront both legal scrutiny and personal remorse. FC Andorra, already battling relegation pressures, will need to rely on a backup keeper for the remainder of the season, a challenge that could further jeopardise their league standing.

As the football world mourns the loss of Jesús de Miguel, the incident serves as a stark reminder that the sport’s physicality must be balanced with rigorous safety measures. The forthcoming weeks will see the federation’s proposed reforms tested, and clubs across Spain will likely reassess their own protocols. Whether this tragedy will catalise lasting change or remain an isolated response remains to be seen, but the call for a safer, more accountable game is now louder than ever.
